what: Howard Hughes Holdings develops master-planned communities, selling land to homebuilders in The Woodlands and Bridgeland near Houston, Summerlin near Las Vegas and Teravalis near Phoenix, and owns offices, retail, apartments and the Ward Village condominium towers in Honolulu. Since 2025 Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square controls it and is turning it into a diversified holding company.
customers: Homebuilders that buy residential lots, condo buyers in Honolulu, and tenants in its offices, shops and apartments.
money: Lots sold to homebuilders, plus builder price participation.
Ward Village towers in Honolulu, booked when towers are completed.
Rents from offices, retail and apartments in its communities.
moat: Huge, low-cost land holdings in fast-growing Sun Belt cities that will take decades to sell, and control over how those communities develop. Land bought long ago becomes more valuable as each community grows.
risks: Earnings are lumpy: condo towers are booked when they close, which can swing a year from profit to loss, as 2023 showed.
Land sales depend on homebuilders, who slow purchases when mortgage rates are high.
The strategy is changing under Pershing Square, which adds uncertainty about how capital will be used.
Only three analysts cover the stock.
opportunities: Cash of $2.9B gives the new owner room to invest or buy back shares.
Operating cash flow of $933M over the last twelve months is large for a $4.6B company.
Land values in Houston, Las Vegas and Phoenix have kept rising.
Pershing Square’s long-term ownership aligns the company with a patient investor.
watch: How Pershing Square deploys the cash, and land sales per acre in Summerlin and Bridgeland.
view: Howard Hughes should be valued on its assets, not its earnings. Land in Summerlin, The Woodlands and Bridgeland, the condo pipeline in Honolulu and the income-producing buildings together are worth far more than reported book value, and a P/E based on whatever condos happened to close this year means very little.

What changed in 2025 is ownership. Pershing Square invested heavily and now intends to use the company as a vehicle for long-term investments, in the way Berkshire Hathaway once grew out of a textile company. That is a bet on Bill Ackman’s capital allocation as much as on Sun Belt land, and his record is strong but uneven.

At $4.6 billion, with $2.9 billion of cash, the market is valuing the land and buildings conservatively. I think the shares are reasonably priced for patient investors, but this is not a land play any more: you are buying into a holding company whose future investments you cannot see yet.
bull: Sun Belt land keeps appreciating and Pershing Square compounds the cash into a Berkshire-style holding company.
bear: Housing slows land sales and the new strategy uses the cash on investments that disappoint.
